Protest
pro-tĕst'
v. (to affirm solemnly; to testify before witnesses; to declare with a warning; rendering Hebrew 'uwd)
Latin protestari, from pro-, before, and testari, to witness — to testify publicly, in the face of all. The modern sense of objection is a narrowing; the Authorized Version keeps the original breadth.

Biblical Definition

To protest in the Authorized Version is not to complain but to swear a thing publicly. Judah reports to Jacob that “the man did solemnly protest unto us, saying, Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you” (Gen 43:3) — Joseph had put the family under a formal declaration. When Israel demanded a king, the LORD told Samuel to give them their way and then to warn them of the cost: “protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king that shall reign over them” (1Sa 8:9). The Hebrew is 'uwd, to testify, to call witnesses, to bear solemn warning — the same root that stands behind the word testimony. Paul takes it up in a great oath of the Christian life: “I protest by your rejoicing which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily” (1Co 15:31), swearing by the joy he had in the church he had begotten that his life was a continual dying. The biblical protest is therefore an oath before God, and the word carries the weight of court and covenant. It is the language of the herald, not of the malcontent. The name Protestant was earned in that older sense: not men who complained, but men who testified.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to protest as to affirm with solemnity; to make a solemn declaration of a fact or opinion; and, of a witness, to declare formally in the face of others.

expand to see more

PROTEST, v.i. To affirm with solemnity; to make a solemn declaration of a fact or opinion.

PROTEST, v.t. To call to witness; to invoke as a witness; also, to prove; to show; to give evidence of.

PROTEST, n. A solemn declaration of opinion, commonly against some act; a formal and public declaration.

Key Scripture

Gen 43:3 — "And Judah spake unto him, saying, The man did solemnly protest unto us, saying, Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you."

1Sa 8:9 — "Now therefore hearken unto their voice: howbeit yet protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king that shall reign over them."

1Co 15:31 — "I protest by your rejoicing which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily."

Modern Corruption

Protest has been emptied of oath and narrowed to grievance, so that the word which once meant to testify for something now means only to be against something.

expand to see more

The English word has travelled a long way downhill. In 1529 the German princes at Speyer entered a protestatio — a formal legal testimony that they could not, before God and conscience, consent to the revocation of the gospel's liberty — and the name Protestant was fastened on the churches of the Reformation from that act. It was a positive word. They were testifying to something: justification by faith alone, the sole authority of Scripture, the crown rights of Christ over His church. Modern usage has reduced protest to the noise a crowd makes when displeased, and the reduction has quietly reshaped how many Protestants understand themselves — as a movement defined by what it left rather than by what it confessed. The corruption is worth naming precisely because it disarms. A church that knows it is protesting for the finished work of Christ has something to say on any day of the week; a church that knows only that it is against Rome has nothing to say once Rome is out of the news. Samuel's protest to Israel is the model: he warned them of the king, and he did it by shewing them the truth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'uwd (H5749), to testify, to bear witness, to warn solemnly; Greek ne (G3513), a particle of strong affirmation, “by” in an oath (1 Corinthians 15:31); compare diamarturomai (G1263), to charge earnestly.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'uwd (H5749) — to testify, to admonish, to warn solemnly; the root behind 'eduth, testimony, the name of the ark's tables; Genesis 43:3, 1 Samuel 8:9.

Greek ne (G3513) — the particle of solemn affirmation, used only once in the New Testament, in Paul's oath by the rejoicing of the Corinthians; 1 Corinthians 15:31.

Greek diamarturomai (G1263) — to testify thoroughly, to charge before God; Paul's word for his own ministry of warning; Acts 20:21, 2 Timothy 4:1.

Usage

"“The man did solemnly protest unto us” — Joseph binding his brothers by a public declaration."

"“Protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king” — the warning that came with the granted request."

"“I protest…I die daily” — Paul's oath on the life of an apostle."
